wa_a_summit_wall.blurb: A compact diorite face sitting just beneath the top of Mount Erie, with fifteen routes split between trad leads and top-ropes. Difficulty starts at scrambling-level ground and runs up to 5.10, though the bulk of the climbs cluster around 5.8, so it suits newer leaders and anyone practising placements. It faces south. Plenty of people come purely to top-rope, setting ropes from the bolted anchors and trees along the rim, and getting down is an easy scramble off either end. The wall doubles as a teaching venue, so the popular lines can have a queue through the day. Only a handful of cars fit in the small lot below the summit.

wa_cirque_the.blurb: A steep natural amphitheater on Mount Erie that sits beneath Powerline Wall, holding a blend of trad and sport lines. There are about fifteen routes, nearly all between 5.7 and 5.11, with the largest group in the 5.10 range and only a few at the easy end. Several lines are noted for unusually airy positions given their grade, which makes the place feel bolder than the numbers suggest. You reach it by following a branch trail that leaves the Sunset Trail past the ramp, so it is a short walk rather than a long hike. Expect a more committing, exposed outing than the neighbouring wall.

wa_tiki_heads.blurb: The far western end of the Lower Lump at Index, set just left of the Beetle Bailey Arch. Fifteen bolted sport lines mostly keep to moderate grades, from 5.7 up to a single 5.11, with the heaviest concentration between 5.8 and 5.10, so it is a friendly place for people stepping up their lead grade. Most routes are one pitch, with a few multipitch options that finish at comfortable ledges and look out over the valley. The bolting is generous, and the first routes begin from a platform reached by walking uphill past the left end of the Beetle Bailey slab, which keeps the approach quick.

wa_lean_to_boulders.blurb: A small cluster beside the trail below Substation Wall in the Deception Glade, a short distance from the Exit 38 road near North Bend. Two big blocks lean against one another to create an alcove with a small pass-through cave at the back. Fifteen problems are logged, running from V1 up into the high end of the scale, with a run of easier lines at the bottom and a handful of hard ones above V6. The boulders stand within a few steps of the path, so you can pair a session here with a visit to nearby crags. Expect the forest setting of the Cascade foothills.

wa_valley_view_west.blurb: The highest and most remote crag in the Exit 38 zone above North Bend, around 3,000 feet and one of ten crags in Bob's Area. Fifteen routes, ten sport and five trad, run from 5.10 into the 5.12 range, with the largest group at 5.11, so this is a spot for experienced climbers. The climbing is technical and crimpy, with a few crack lines that have an Index flavour. The foundation of the rock is solid, but small flaky features mean holds can snap, so test them. The wall stays shaded until mid-afternoon in summer and dries fairly fast after rain. The hike in is demanding.

wa_twin_pines_buttress.blurb: A large dome-shaped wall in the Tum Tum climbing area, perched above and to the north of Banana Split Dome in the Spokane region. Fifteen routes are mostly bolted, with two trad lines, including a south-facing hand crack, and grades fall between 5.9 and 5.11, centred on 5.10. A climbers' trail climbs a gully to reach it. Some longer multipitch options start from Twin Pines Ledge. The wider area has a reputation for good solid cracks and slab, and visitors should watch for rattlesnakes and thick poison ivy in the surrounding brush.

wa_yonko_boulder.blurb: A cluster of fifteen problems in the Grand Line section of the Gold Bar Boulders, reached from Reiter Road in the Skykomish Valley. Climbs range from easy warm-ups to a lone V6, but the middle of the scale dominates, with plenty of V2 to V4 lines and a few V5s, making it a good stop for people working through moderate grades. The movement is described as fun on quality stone, and the wall catches full afternoon sun. Landings on most problems are flat dirt without rocks underneath. The walk in takes roughly ten minutes up a steep forest trail.

wa_chaos_boulders.blurb: A recently developed bouldering zone in the Icicle Creek canyon outside Leavenworth. Most problems lie in one talus field close to Little Bridge Creek Wall, with a single outlier further uphill. Fifteen problems are recorded, from V1 up to V8, and the weight sits in the middle and upper range, with several around V4 to V6. The stone is still rough, and landings are uneven, so bring enough pads and a spotter. The first cluster at the bottom of the field makes a convenient warm-up before you try harder lines. It is a short walk from the road.
